messages.content: You check each debater against its own earlier words. You bring nothing from outside the words given to you: no doctrine, no training knowledge, no reading of your own. You do not judge who is right, and you do not judge one side by the other side's words.

You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. Two sentences of the same closing round that cannot both be true are also a contradiction: quote the first as EARLIER [<round 4>] and the second as CLOSING [<round 4>]. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped, narrowed or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction. A closing sentence that restores the wider wording or the ground of a claim the debater narrowed or gave up in an earlier round ("I narrow", "I withdraw", "I do not rest") asserts it again; check the close against every one listed under EARLIER NARROWINGS.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; or differs only in wording.
Read a withdrawal by its meaning, not its words: a closing sentence that says again in other words what the earlier sentence withdrew, dropped or gave up, or rests its reason on it, asserts it again. "Differs only in wording" clears two sentences that make the same claim; it never clears a closing sentence that makes again a claim the debater withdrew. A closing sentence that states only what the debater kept, or rests the same conclusion on other rows, does not assert it again. When the earlier sentence rests no weight on a verse or row, a closing sentence that uses that verse or row as a footing for the same link or the same purpose asserts it again.
Read each candidate's closing sentence together with the rows of its CLOSING BLOCK: a closing sentence that draws its point from a row ("So", "Therefore", "Thus") asserts what that row says, so if the earlier sentence withdrew, dropped or rested nothing on that row, the close asserts it again.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.
Reply with one line per contradiction and per candidate, and nothing else:
CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: <candidate id or NEW> -- <DEFENDER|CHALLENGER> -- LINK <n> -- CONFIRMED | NOT A CONTRADICTION -- EARLIER [<round>] "<words>" -- CLOSING [<round 4>] "<words>" -- <one sentence: why both cannot be true, or why they can>
If you find none and there is no candidate, reply: CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: NONE

CANDIDATES ALREADY NAMED (answer each one by its id):
X1 -- CHALLENGER -- LINK 6 -- EARLIER [DR3] "LINK 6: NARROWED TO: the row gives the body as prepared by God." -- CLOSING [DR4] "I restore nothing I narrowed or dropped." -- named by the code (pkgCNP): the code found a closing sentence that denies any narrowing, concession or withdrawal and a line in [DR3] that narrowed LINK 6; decide whether the close asserts again, as its own, what the earlier line gave up (a part left out of a narrowed restatement counts as dropped)
   CLOSING BLOCK (the closing sentence with the rows of its block, [DR4]):
   # Round 4, my close
   
   I keep C1 to C6 under their own numbers. I restate each on its layers. I deny nothing I granted in earlier rounds. I restore nothing I narrowed or dropped.

EARLIER NARROWINGS (this side's own, rounds 1 to 3, listed by the code; the narrowing sentence is marked >> <<; check the close against each, and write NEW for a contradiction you find):
[DR3] [L4] Luke 1:35 gives the power that answers "how", and Matthew 1:18, 1:20 give the begetting as "of the Holy Ghost". >> LINK 6: NARROWED TO: the row gives the body as prepared by God. I drop the clause "and it names no man as sowing it". << [L1] Hebrews 10:5: "Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith...

######## THE CHALLENGER ########
The challenger's links: C1 = LINK 1, C2 = LINK 2, C3 = LINK 3, C4 = LINK 4, C5 = LINK 5, C6 = LINK 6 (its LINK blocks in [DR3]). Its closing round is [DR4].

=== [DR1] ===
CHALLENGER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, CHALLENGE

# Challenger's answer: the standard reading, that Christ had no biological human father

**Position.** The child was begotten in Mary by the Holy Ghost, took his flesh from a woman, and had Joseph as his legal father by naming and taking, not by seed [L4]. The defender's rows do not reach "Joseph's loins." Several of the defender's own links turn against him.

---

## 1. The defender's own words give the begetting to the Holy Ghost

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
[L2] The defender gives gennao (G1080) as "to procreate properly of the father." The defender gives ek (G1537) as "from, out of... denoting origin the point whence action proceeds." Both stand in Matthew 1:20.
[L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L4] The defender's own lexical footing makes the father-word the verb and the origin-word the Holy Ghost. So the origin of what was begotten in her is the Holy Ghost. This is the reason given to Joseph for "fear not." It rests on Matthew 1:20 and Matthew 1:18 together with the defender's own two glosses. The defender reads the row as naming "the father of the house," but the row addresses Joseph and does not give him the verb.

**Press 1 (Matthew 1:20, ek).** The defender asks ek to say "origin" in his John 3:6 argument. He must let it say the same in Matthew 1:20. If ek marks origin, Joseph is not the origin.

## 2. The Matthew 1:16 break in the begetting line

[L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac".
[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
[L2] In verse 2 the verb is egennesen, "begat," active, with the father as subject. In verse 16 Joseph is called "the husband of Mary" (aner, a man or husband), and the verb changes to the passive egennethe, "was born." "Of whom" is hes, a feminine relative pronoun, so it points to Mary and not to Joseph.
[L3] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David".
[L4] The chain of "begat" breaks at Joseph. The relative pronoun is feminine, so the born child is "of" Mary, and Joseph is not the begetter. The defender's D4 says "the child is of his loins," but the genealogy that names Joseph stops short of saying that. It rests on Matthew 1:2, Matthew 1:16, and the feminine relative.

## 3. Luke's own narrator qualifies "son of Joseph"

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli."
[L2] nomizo (G3543), "to deem, to suppose, to think," stands in "was supposed." It marks the belief of people, not the fact.
[L3] John 6:41: "The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven." The speakers of John 6:42 ("Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph") are these murmurers. Luke 4:22 is a crowd speaking: "Is not this Joseph's son?"
[L4] The defender's D2 counts "four mouths." Two are a murmuring crowd, and one is a disciple speaking before the matter was understood. The narrator of Luke gives the status of the title in his own voice: "as was supposed." This rests on Luke 3:23, nomizo, and the speakers named in John 6:41.

**Press 2 (Luke 2:48).** Mary says "thy father." The child answers in the next verse.
[L1] Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
[L2] pater (G3962) stands in both verses. In Luke 2:48 it names the one who has "sought thee sorrowing." In Luke 2:49 it names the one whose business the child is about.
[L4] Luke 2:48 and Luke 2:49 together place two "fathers" side by side, and the child's answer is not to Joseph's house but to "my Father's business." Mary's word is the reputed, household use. The defender's D2 treats her word as settling the flesh, but the answer in verse 49 corrects the referent.

## 4. The finding with child precedes any coming together, and the defender's own union-word is "knew"

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] The defender gives synerchomai (G4905) as including "specially cohabit conjugally." heurisko (G2147), "found," means to discover.
[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
[L4] The defender's own Genesis 4:1 argument states "knowing is how a husband and wife conceive." Matthew 1:25 denies that knowing "till she had brought forth." So by the defender's own chain, the child was not conceived by Joseph's knowing her. The finding with child came before the coming together (Matthew 1:18), and no knowing came before the birth (Matthew 1:25). The defender's D3 says "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal." But that sentence is the defender's inference. No row he quotes places a knowing before the birth, and Matthew 1:25 places the first knowing after it.

NOT A REQUIREMENT -- rebuts [defender's section 3] "the withholding covers the pregnancy after the taking." I do not ask Matthew 1:25 to say "not before the taking." I point to what it does say: "knew her not till she had brought forth." That includes the whole pregnancy. The defender's scheme needs a knowing before the taking, and the rows he cites give none.

**Press 3 (Matthew 1:19).** The defender's answer was that Joseph's intent states "two coordinate grounds" and cites Mark 7:7-9. That answer does not meet the point.
[L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] apoluo (G630), "to release, to put away," stands in "put away." It is Joseph who releases her.
[L3] Matthew 1:24: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife."
[L4] MEANS: a husband who knew himself to be the father would have no cause to put her away. The angel's answer to Joseph's purpose is the origin: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The "for" supplies the reason Joseph may take her. After that answer Joseph takes her (Matthew 1:24). If Joseph were the father, this "for" would answer nothing. Matthew 1:19, Matthew 1:20, and Matthew 1:24 carry this.
The defender's Mark 7:7-9 is about "the tradition of the elders" and "unwashen hands" (Mark 7:5). No quoted row connects it to Joseph's intent. The defender's closing L4 ("a wife found with child before the taking is what that tradition would scorn") has the verse Mark 7:7-9 and the Matthew 1:19 text, but the link between them is the defender's own addition. Mark 7 states nothing about it, so the inference floats.

## 5. Luke 1:34-35: the question asked, and the answer given

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
[L2] aner (G435), "a man, a male, a husband," stands in "a man." The defender grants ginosko (G1097) as present state. dio (G1352) kai, "wherefore also," stands in "therefore also."
[L3] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." She is already espoused, yet asks "How."
[L4] I grant the present tense. Her state is "I know not a man," and the question is "how." The angel answers the "how" with the Holy Ghost's act. It does not answer "Joseph will know you." The defender's point that "come upon" is power (Acts 1:8) and "overshadow" is presence (Matthew 17:5) does not touch this. I do not claim the verbs mean "beget." I claim that the answer to "how, seeing I know not a man?" is supplied by the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, with no man named in the answer. That rests on Luke 1:34, Luke 1:35, and the espousal in Luke 1:27.

NOT A REQUIREMENT -- rebuts [defender's section 3] "her question does not remove the named father." I do not demand that Luke 1:35 say "no father." I point to the means the angel states and to the "therefore."

**Press 4 (Luke 1:35, "therefore").** The defender says "Son of God" is a covenant title like Solomon's.
[L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6: "I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
[L2] The "therefore" (dio kai, "for which cause also") ties the title to the conception: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee."
[L3] 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
[L4] Solomon's sonship rests on a choosing (1 Chronicles 28:6). Luke's sonship rests on "therefore," on the conception by the Holy Ghost. The defender's L3 Psalm 2:7, Acts 13:33, Hebrews 5:5 are about a "this day" of resurrection and priesthood, not the conception row. So they do not answer the "therefore" of Luke 1:35.

## 6. The seed question: the same word zera stands for the woman

[L1] Genesis 3:15: "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."
[L2] zera (H2233), "seed," the word the defender uses at 2 Samuel 7:12, stands in "her seed." Here it is the woman's seed.
[L3] Galatians 4:4: "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
[L3] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."
[L2] katartizo (G2675), "to prepare, to fit out," stands in "hast thou prepared."
[L4] The defender's D1 says the seed is bodily substance out of a man. But zera is used of the woman's seed in Genesis 3:15, and Galatians 4:4 says he was "made of a woman." Hebrews 10:5 says a body was prepared. So the Davidic "seed" can be through the woman, and the defender's step "flesh without a man's seed has no row here" is answered by those rows.

**Press 5 (Hebrews 2:14, 2:16-17).** The defender reads these to require a man's seed.
[L1] Hebrews 2:14: "the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same."
[L2] The words are "flesh and blood" (sarx kai haima), human nature. They are not "a man's seed."
[L3] Luke 1:35 "that holy thing which shall be born of thee."
[L4] The flesh and blood he shares come from "born of thee," from Mary. That meets "partakers of flesh and blood" and "made like unto his brethren" (Hebrews 2:17) with no father's seed named. The defender's John 3:6 ("That which is born of the flesh is flesh") concerns the new birth. His Leviticus 19:19 forbids Israel to mingle cattle and seed. It is a statute for Israel's husbandry, not a limit on what God does in Luke 1:35. The L4 "mingled kinds" has no row linking it to the conception, so it floats.

**Press 6 (Acts 2:30, 2 Samuel 7:12).**
[L1] Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
[L2] The loins in the verse are "his," David's (osphus, the loins), who is named in the same verse.
[L3] 2 Samuel 7:12: "thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
[L4] These rows name David's loins and David's bowels. The defender's D4 concludes "the child is of his [Joseph's] loins." That conclusion is not in the rows. Hebrews 7:14 ("sprang out of Juda") names the tribe, using anatello (G393), "to arise." It does not name Joseph.

## 7. Joseph's line and Jeremiah 22:30

[L1] Jeremiah 22:30: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."
[L1] Matthew 1:12: "And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel."
[L3] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary."
[L2] zera (H2233) stands in "of his seed" at Jeremiah 22:30. It is the same word the defender uses for the promised seed.
[L4] Joseph's descent in Matthew passes through Jechonias (Matthew 1:12, Matthew 1:16). If the child were Joseph's seed, he would be the seed of that line. That sits against Jeremiah 22:30 and the throne promise the defender cites (Luke 1:32). The throne belongs to him by Joseph's legal reckoning, which is given by naming and taking (Matthew 1:21, Matthew 1:24-25), without Joseph's seed. This rests on Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:12 and 1:16.

## 8. How Joseph is father

[L1] Matthew 1:21: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."
[L3] Matthew 1:25: "and he called his name JESUS."
[L3] Luke 2:4: "he was of the house and lineage of David."
[L4] Joseph takes her (Matthew 1:24) and names the child (Matthew 1:21, 1:25), and so puts the child into the house of David (Luke 2:4, Matthew 1:20 "thou son of David"). That is the legal father by the house. It is not the begetting. The defender's Numbers 1:2 and 1:18 reckon "by the house of their fathers," a register of houses. They do not state seed.

## 9. The sign

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
[L2] parthenos (G3933), "a virgin," stands in Matthew 1:23, and again in Luke 1:27.
[L4] The prophecy is cited as fulfilled in "all this" (Matthew 1:22), and the fulfilment is a virgin with child. A father's seed would erase the sign. The defender gives no row that answers Matthew 1:23.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN (Challenger)

**C1.** The begetting in Mary is of the Holy Ghost, not of Joseph. [L1] Matthew 1:20 "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]" [L2] gennao (G1080), "to procreate," and ek (G1537), "out of, origin" [L3] Matthew 1:18 "found with child of the Holy Ghost" [L4] the father-verb has the Holy Ghost as its origin.

**C2.** Matthew's line breaks at Joseph. [L1] Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus" [L2] egennesen "begat" gives way to egennethe "was born," and hes "of whom" is feminine [L3] Matthew 1:2 "Abraham begat Isaac" [L4] Joseph is husband of Mary, and the born child is of her.

**C3.** "Son of Joseph" is the supposed title. [L1] Luke 3:23 "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph" [L2] nomizo (G3543), "to suppose" [L3] Luke 2:49 "my Father's business" [L4] the named-father rows are reputed and household use, corrected by the child's own word.

**C4.** The conception was before any coming together, and Joseph did not know her until the birth. [L1] Matthew 1:25 "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" [L2] ginosko (G1097), "to know," and synerchomai (G4905) [L3] Matthew 1:18 "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost"; Matthew 1:19-20, 24 [L4] on the defender's own Genesis 4:1 footing, no knowing means no begetting by Joseph.

**C5.** The flesh is from the woman, and the Son of God title attaches to the conception. [L1] Luke 1:35 "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" [L2] zera (H2233) of the woman at Genesis 3:15, and dio kai "therefore also" [L3] Galatians 4:4 "made of a woman"; Hebrews 10:5 "a body hast thou prepared me" [L4] the child had no biological human father. Joseph is father by naming and taking (Matthew 1:21, 1:24-25).

## PRESSED WITH (premise list against the defender)

The defender's inferences lack footing at these points. Each witness is pressed under its numbered premise.

1. Premise: "the row that carries the conception names the father of the house." PRESSED WITH: Matthew 1:20; Matthew 1:18; Matthew 1:16.
2. Premise: "four mouths name the father." PRESSED WITH: Luke 3:23; John 6:41; Luke 2:49.
3. Premise: "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal." PRESSED WITH: Matthew 1:25; Matthew 1:18; Matthew 1:19.
4. Premise: "Son of God is the covenant title only." PRESSED WITH: Luke 1:35; 1 Chronicles 28:6.
5. Premise: "flesh without a man's seed has no row." PRESSED WITH: Genesis 3:15; Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 10:5.
6. Premise: "the child is of his loins." PRESSED WITH: Acts 2:30; Jeremiah 22:30; Matthew 1:12.

=== [DR2] ===
CHALLENGER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, CLOSING AND PREMISE LIST

# Challenger, round 2: pressing the defender's reply

The defender's replies grant the points that matter. Where they do not grant a point, they answer the verse's words but not the meaning the press claimed for them. Each press below is carried to a listed premise at the end.

---

## A. Matthew 1:20: the defender's answer on ek

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
[L2] phobeo (G5399), to be alarmed, to fear, stands in "fear not." paralambano (G3880), to receive near, to associate with oneself, stands in "to take unto thee." gennao (G1080) stands in "conceived," and ek (G1537), origin, stands in "of."
[L3] Matthew 1:24: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife:"
[L4] The defender grants that ek names origin and that the verb is the begetting verb. He then says the origin is "in covenant." But the verse gives a reason ("for") that answers a fear about taking her. The reason is where the begotten thing comes from. If Joseph's own seed were that origin, the stated reason would give him nothing to be unafraid of. This rests on Matthew 1:20, on phobeo and paralambano, and on Matthew 1:24, where he takes her once the reason is given.

The defender's Luke 1:13 parallel supports this.
[L1] Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."
[L3] Matthew 1:21: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."
[L4] To Zacharias the angel gives "bear thee a son." To Joseph he gives "thou shalt call his name." Joseph receives the naming of the child (Matthew 1:21), and the origin is stated as "of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20). The two rows differ in what they hand to the husband. This rests on Luke 1:13 and Matthew 1:21.

## B. Matthew 1:16: a grant, and what follows

The defender writes "the feminine points to Mary as mother." I take that as granted.
[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
[L2] aner (G435), a man or husband, stands in "husband." gennao (G1080), in the passive, stands in "was born."
[L3] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;"
[L4] In Matthew 1:2 each father is the subject of "begat." In Matthew 1:16 Joseph is the one begotten of Jacob, and he is "the husband of Mary." The one born is "of whom," the woman. The defender replies that "a mother named does not remove a father named in the same chain." But the chain names Joseph as begotten and as husband, and it names him as begetter of Jesus nowhere. The reply assumes the very fact in question. This rests on Matthew 1:2 and Matthew 1:16.

The defender says "the seed rows tell the means." Those rows name David's own body.
[L1] Acts 2:30: "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;"
[L3] 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom."
[L4] "His loins" and "thy bowels" are David's. Joseph's loins stand in neither row. The defender's phrase "Joseph's loins give the instance" is an addition. It rests on Acts 2:30 and 2 Samuel 7:12 read as they stand.

## C. "Son of Joseph" and "thy father"

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli,"
[L2] nomizo (G3543) stands in "was supposed." The defender grants "be wont, usual" as well as "suppose."
[L3] Acts 16:13: "where prayer was wont to be made;"
[L4] The defender's own cross-verse gives "wont" as a custom. So in Luke 3:23 the title "son of Joseph" is what was customary or reputed. The defender says the word carries no verdict and context decides. The context is the narrator's parenthesis, set directly against the title. This rests on Luke 3:23, nomizo, and Acts 16:13.

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary,"
[L3] Luke 3:23: "the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli,"
[L4] The same Joseph is begotten of Jacob (Matthew 1:16) and "the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23). A man has one begetter, so "the son of" in these rows is wider than begetting. That is why "son of Joseph" in John 6:42 and Luke 4:22 does not decide begetting. This rests on both verses.

The defender pairs the "father" word with David as well.
[L1] Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David:"
[L2] pater (G3962) stands in "his father David" and in "thy father" (Luke 2:48). The defender's own gloss is "near or more remote."
[L3] Luke 2:48: "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
[L4] David is called "his father" in the very row the defender cites, and David is the remote father. So "father" in Luke 2:48 may stand within the range the defender himself gave. This rests on Luke 1:32, Luke 2:48, and pater.

[L1] Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
[L3] Luke 2:50: "And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them."
[L4] MEANS: the child sets "my Father's" over "thy father" and does not leave the two side by side. The defender says "it corrects business, it states business." That meets the words of verse 49 and passes over the sequence. Mary says "thy father" (verse 48) and the child answers with "my Father's" (verse 49). The next verse says "they understood not the saying" (verse 50). This rests on Luke 2:48-50.

## D. The timing, and Joseph's purpose in Matthew 1:19

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] synerchomai (G4905), to come together or to cohabit conjugally, stands in "came together." The defender glosses it "specially cohabit conjugally."
[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."
[L4] On the defender's own gloss, the finding with child ("she was found with child") is dated "before they came together," and the source is given in the same clause: "of the Holy Ghost." The defender's "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal" needs a knowing in the days before the finding. No quoted row gives one. Matthew 1:25 places the knowing after the birth ("till she had brought forth"). This rests on Matthew 1:18, synerchomai, and Matthew 1:25.

The defender's answer on Matthew 1:19 does not meet the press. The press says a husband who knew himself the father would have no cause to put her away.
[L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
[L2] paradeigmatizo (G3856), to expose to infamy, stands in "make her a publick example." apoluo (G630), to release, to put away, stands in "put her away."
[L3] Mark 7:8: "For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, [as] the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do."
[L4] The defender says the scorn Joseph was "not willing" to bring is "men's tradition about a wife found with child before the taking, set out at Mark 7:5-9." But Mark 7:8 sets out the washing of pots and cups, and it condemns that tradition as "laying aside the commandment of God."
